nameStory: Colts-foot gets its charming name from the shape of its leaves, which resemble the rounded hoof print of a young horse or colt. The leaves are heart-shaped to kidney-shaped with a distinctive cleft where they attach to the stem, creating that unmistakable "hoof" silhouette that early botanists couldn't help but notice.
description: Colts-foot is a low-growing perennial herb that produces bright yellow, dandelion-like flowers on scaly stems in early spring, often while snow still lingers. The flowers appear before the leaves, which is unusual and helps make this plant memorable. The large, soft leaves emerge later in spring and can grow 4-8 inches across, staying close to the ground in a basal rosette. This European native has naturalized throughout New England and rarely grows taller than 6-12 inches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers appear in early spring on purplish, scaly stems before any leaves emerge - this 'flowers first, leaves later' timing is the key identification feature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges emerge after flowering, feeling soft and woolly underneath with a distinctive white felt-like texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that forms colonies from underground runners, with leaves arranged in basal rosettes close to the ground

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are covered in overlapping, purplish-brown scales that feel papery to the touch, resembling tiny shingles on a roof

habitat: Look for colts-foot along roadsides, disturbed soils, stream banks, and waste places throughout New England. It thrives in moist, clay-rich soils and is often found in areas with poor drainage where other plants struggle. This adaptable plant is particularly common in urban and suburban areas, spreading along ditches and embankments.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flowers bloom from March to May on scaly stems, often pushing through late snow. The distinctive heart-shaped leaves emerge after the flowers fade, growing rapidly through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Only the large, soft leaves are visible, forming low mats of heart-shaped foliage. The white, woolly undersides of leaves are most noticeable during dry summer days.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow and begin to die back, though some may persist into early winter in protected spots.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground roots and runners, with no above-ground parts visible until the next spring's flower emergence.

funFact: Colts-foot flowers bloom and often finish flowering completely before producing a single leaf - it's like the plant is playing a botanical game of peek-a-boo, showing you its cheerful yellow face before revealing its true leafy identity weeks later!
confusionNotes: The early spring flowers are easily confused with dandelions, but colts-foot flowers appear on scaly, leafless stems while dandelion flowers always have jagged leaves present at the base. Memory trick: 'Colts-foot shows flowers first, leaves second - dandelions show both together.'
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Tussilago comes from the Latin words for 'cough' and 'to act on,' reflecting its traditional use as a cough remedy. However, modern science has discovered that colts-foot contains potentially harmful compounds, so it should never be used medicinally despite its historical reputation as a healing herb.
compareHints: Colts-foot is the only species in its genus Tussilago, making it unique in the sunflower family for its distinctive 'flowers before leaves' habit. While other early spring members of the Asteraceae family like dandelions also have yellow flowers, none share colts-foot's unusual timing of leafless flowering stems followed by the emergence of large, heart-shaped basal leaves.
